lesson_title: The Six Hundredth Vetkoek: Paper 2 in One Stall
hook_text: Vetkoek number six hundred earns nothing at all — and it is the most important one of the month.
clip_script: A vetkoek stall at the taxi rank. Each vetkoek eats six rand before it earns a cent — flour, oil, filling, gas, the paper packet. Those costs ride on every single one: make ten, spend sixty; make a hundred, spend six hundred. But the stall spot and the gas bottle want two thousand four hundred rand a month whether it rains all week or the queue never ends. Two kinds of cost: the ones that travel, and the ones that sit. She sells at ten rand. So each vetkoek, after feeding itself, drops four rand toward that stubborn rent. Four rand — the contribution. How many four-rand payments cover two thousand four hundred? Six hundred. Vetkoek number six hundred is the break-even vetkoek: the moment the stall stops owing and starts earning. It makes no profit itself — it just opens the gate. From six hundred and one onward, the full four rand is hers. She usually sells nine hundred: three hundred past the line, times four — twelve hundred rand of profit. Now watch what the examiner watches: flour spikes, each vetkoek eats seven rand, contribution thins to three, and suddenly the rent needs eight hundred sales. She feels her break-even move the week prices move. That instinct — contribution against fixed costs — is the entire factory question in Paper 2, wearing an apron.
visual_style: A queue of glowing vetkoek marching toward a rent wall, each dropping a four-rand coin into a rising meter; the six hundredth one lights the wall green; a flour price spike shrinks the coins to three rand and the wall stretches further away.
pacing: Quick sorting of the two cost kinds, steady coin-drop build to the green light, sharp jolt at the flour spike.
call_to_action: Watch the full revision session and carry break-even, budgets, reconciliations and VAT into Paper 2 in one sweep.
